extracted.intended_audience: math olympiad students, coaches, and advanced high-school/early-undergraduate problem solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and heuristics for solving olympiad-style number theory and combinatorics problems (digit expansions, residues, invariants, exponential Diophantine methods, numerical functional equations). Contains worked examples and problem lists illustrating each method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use base expansions to convert recurrences into digit-operations
rubrics_metrics.description: When recurrences or definitions involve multiplying by the base and adding constants (e.g., f(2n) and f(2n+1)), write numbers in that base so multiplication by the base corresponds to a shift of digits and additions correspond to digit changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show by induction that f(n) equals the number of 1’s in the binary expansion when f(1)=1 and f(2n)=f(n), f(2n+1)=f(n)+1. More generally, map binary digits read in one base to digits read in another base (e.g., read base-2 digits as base-3 digits) to get closed forms for f. Use induction on the digit decomposition; check even/odd (2n vs 2n+1) separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound digit-statistics by comparing to powers of base
rubrics_metrics.description: To find maxima/minima of quantities that count digits (e.g., number of 1’s in binary for n ≤ N), compare N to powers of the base to get an upper bound on the number of digits (and thus on the count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: since 1994 < 2^{11}-1, any number ≤1994 has at most 10 binary digits equal to 1, and 1023 (all ten 1’s) attains 10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read decimal (or other base) expansions to construct functions with desired topological properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode information in the digits of x (decimal expansion) to explicitly construct functions (or pairs of functions) with the intermediate value property or other surjectivity properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sierpiński’s construction splitting decimal digits into two subsequences ax_n and bx_n, using eventual periodic patterns to define g and h with the intermediate value property and g+h=f. The guidance emphasizes reading digits far down the expansion to control values locally and achieve surjectivity on intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use residues modulo 9 to relate digit sums and detect growth patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum-of-digits is congruent modulo 9 to the original number. Periodicity of residues (e.g., S(2^n) modulo 9) can be used to force contradictions about monotonicity or growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: residues of S(2^n) modulo 9 repeat as 1,2,4,8,7,5; assuming eventual monotonic increase gives a lower bound per period that contradicts an upper linear bound on S(2^n). Compute per-period increases adding multiples of 9 when residues drop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply divisibility-by-11 via alternating digit sums for counting/permutation problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A base-10 integer is divisible by 11 iff the alternating sum of its digits is divisible by 11. Use this to classify tuples/digit permutations that can be arranged to be divisible by 11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: count k-tuples whose digits can be permuted to give a number divisible by 11. Use transformations (add constant to all digits; multiply by scalar modulo 11) to map between A(2m) and A(2m-1) and show cardinality relations like A(2m)=10 A(2m-1). Note: ensure transformed digits remain valid (0–9) by checking residues modulo 11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem for modular reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standard theorems (a^p ≡ a (mod p), a^{φ(n)} ≡ 1 (mod n) for gcd(a,n)=1) to reduce large powers modulo primes or composite moduli and to construct congruence relations that show divisibility or periodicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: show infinitely many numbers of the form 33...31 divisible by 31 using 10^{30} ≡ 1 (mod 31); use Euler/Fermat to find residues of exponentials needed in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use residues of numerators to evaluate sums of fractional parts {kp/q}
rubrics_metrics.description: For coprime p and q, the fractional part {kp/q} equals (residue of kp modulo q)/q. The residues k*p mod q form a permutation of 1..q-1; summing their fractions yields combinatorial reciprocity results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sum_{k=1}^{q-1} {kp/q} = (q-1)/2 and reciprocity sum_{k=1}^{q-1} {kp/q} + sum_{k=1}^{p-1} {kq/p} = (p-1)(q-1)/2. Use permutation of residues because gcd(p,q)=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert exponential Diophantine equations into congruences to bound exponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Study parity and residues of exponentials (e.g., 3^x - 1 modulo small powers of 2) to bound the exponent of a prime dividing an expression, thus restricting possible exponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: factor 3^x - 1 as product of (3^{2^t * odd} - 1) factors to count 2-adic valuation, derive inequality x ≤ m+2 then check small m values. This yields finite case checks for possible x,y solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pythagorean triple parametrization when equation reduces to sum of two squares equals a square
rubrics_metrics.description: If an equation can be rearranged into X^2 + Y^2 = Z^2 with X,Y,Z pairwise coprime (and Y even), apply the classical parametrization X = u^2 - v^2, Y = 2uv, Z = u^2 + v^2 to deduce arithmetic constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from 3^{x}+4^{y}=5^{z} deduce X=3^{x1}, Y=2^{y}, Z=5^{z1}, then use parametrization to show u,v must be powers of 2 and proceed to limit possibilities. Combine parity/divisibility arguments to finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization and cyclotomic-like factor product analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When facing expressions like a^{n} - 1, factor them into products of terms (a^{d} - 1) to analyze prime/exponent contributions and derive valuations of primes (e.g., exponent of 2), which give inequalities on unknown exponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: write 3^{x}-1 = Π (3^{2^k * odd} - 1) to estimate 2-adic valuation; deduce bounds like x ≤ m+2 and reduce to small cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greedy/least-number construction for sequences defined by avoidance conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences defined recursively by choosing the least integer greater than previous that avoids forming certain patterns (e.g., arithmetic progression of fixed length, or avoids being in the image union pairwise sums), build the sequence greedily and prove uniqueness by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sequence defined to avoid arithmetic progressions of length p yields rule: write n in base p-1 and read in base p. Another example: when the set of excluded numbers at stage n is known, f(n) is the least number > f(n-1) not in the excluded set; this uniquely determines f step-by-step (used to derive closed form floor-type expressions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use monotonicity, multiplicativity and prime divisibility to pin down numerical functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine increasing/surjectivity/multiplicative conditions with prime factor arguments to show that f(n)=n (or other canonical forms) is the only solution to functional equations on N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: assuming f(mn)=f(m)f(n) for coprime m,n and increasing with f(2)=2, deduce f(n)=n by checking primes and multiplicativity; use divisibility and square conditions (f(n) square for all n) to deduce linear/quadratic forms and then force parameters by primality constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply bounding + iterative/inductive step with a fixed period to solve functional equations involving iterates
rubrics_metrics.description: When an equation involves iterates f^{(k)} and linear combinations (e.g., f^{(19)}(n)+97 f(n)=98n+232), first get uniform bounds on f(n) for small ranges, then use an induction with a step equal to a period (here 36) to prove f(n)=n+2 globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show f(n) ≤ n+3 for n ≤ 156 then deduce f(n)=n+2 for n ≤ 36 via inequalities; then use iterate substitutions and induction with step 36 to extend to all n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use invariants (colorings, group-valued products, residue sums) to prove impossibility of transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate to configurations (boards, polynomials, arrays) quantities that are preserved by allowed moves (parity/color of last square, product in Klein four group, residue of sum modulo small modulus). If initial and target configurations have different invariant values, the transformation is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: knight's tour parity/color invariant excludes visiting opposite corner; checker removal uses Klein four group product of square-colors to show final single-checker configuration impossible; 3×7 subarray sum modulo 3 invariant blocks turning rows into arithmetic progressions. Choose invariant adapted to allowed moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design group-valued invariants for combinatorial move-sets
rubrics_metrics.description: When parity/string-based invariants are insufficient, map squares/elements to elements of a small group (e.g., Klein four) and take product/sum over occupied positions; show the move corresponds to multiplication by identity so product is invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: label board squares by group elements a,b,c,e so that a move multiplies the global product by e; initial product e implies lower bounds on final number of pieces. The technique generalizes to other finite groups chosen to match move symmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit local-to-global digit control: modify tail of an expansion to achieve local values
rubrics_metrics.description: To get desired function values between two reals or to ensure surjectivity on intervals, alter sufficiently long tail digits of the decimal expansion of x to control g(x),h(x) while keeping x between given endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Sierpiński construction: by changing digits starting at some far position one can achieve any prescribed finite sequence of digits for ax_k and bx_k and hence realize any target values for g and h on a subinterval; this shows restrictions of g and h to intervals are surjective and gives the intermediate value property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use permutation and modular-linear transforms to relate digit-multisets across lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply operations (add same integer to all digits; multiply digits by scalar modulo base+1 etc.) that preserve the property of being permutable to a divisible-by-criterion to construct bijections between admissible tuples of different lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the mod-11 divisibility counting, given a 2m-tuple with a permutation giving alternating sum 0 mod 11, adding 1 then multiplying by appropriate l modulo 11 produces a (2m-1)-tuple, establishing a 10-to-1 correspondence between A(2m) and A(2m-1). Verify transformed entries are valid digits.
